utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor vs. Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Madam Registrar. Mr. Hansen, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to continue? I would like to advise the parties that the Chamber has in mind that we'll be able to conclude the testimony of this witness today and there will be some time left to make submissions on sedating in relation to 98 bis. We have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that after re-booting the system, it's functioning again. The case was called by Madam Registrar, and we had technical difficulties, and I have reminded Mr. Hansen that he is still bound by the solemn declaration he gave at the beginning of his testimony. And finally I invited you, Mr. Hedaraly, to resume your examination-in-chief after I had advised the parties that the Chamber expects to conclude the testimony of this witness today and that even some time would remain. That is also the reason why the Chamber has decided that we would have a less than usual lunch break in order to avoid any risk that we would have to ask Mr. Hansen to stay over the weekend. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We left off yesterday talking about the looting in Knin on the 7th and 8th of August when you left the UN camp for the first time. Do you remember that discussion we had?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me go to your third statement, which is P1285. That's tab 3 in your binder. At paragraph 10, the next-to-last sentence you say: "I remember that in Knin I saw on houses -- I saw signs on houses saying something like, Croat houses, do not touch." Now, can you please tell the Court how many of these signs you saw in Knin, whether that was a regular occurrence or just one incident?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I do not remember the exact number, I saw a number of houses, so it was a regular occurrence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would you be able to provide the Trial Chamber with any estimate, just whatever you would feel comfortable as being accurate.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I saw them wherever I went. I did not, or course, see them where I did not go. And I would assume maybe 20, 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hansen. In the same paragraph, you are also saying that looting was committed by both military and civilian persons. Can you give the Court any information as to whether there was a sequence to the looting?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the very beginning from our -- from the time we stayed in the southern barracks, we could see what unfolded just outside the main gate and the looting that took place at that point was conducted by combat troops. And that means up until about the 8th. And at that time we were able to leave the camp and patrolling the streets and -- and the -- the urban areas and the rural areas, we noticed that the combat troop had left, were replaced by a different kind of troops, and we saw also police involved. So from this point on, there was a -- a different dynamics of the looting, and that went on until I left Knin at about the 17th, 18th. I then came back in the beginning of September, and at that point, a noticeable change was that a lot of civilians were involved also. So to my recollection, I see about three waves in this campaign. First, the first four or five days after the Storm operation, looting conducted by combat troops from about the 8th, 9th, until the 17th, uniformed personnel mainly and that continued up until the 17th, and then when he came back also civilians were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify. When you say uniformed personnel, are you referring to troops or to police or to both?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To both, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me change topics slightly and show you P830 which is in tab 6 of your binder. And we'll come back to this document as well later, but for now I just want to focus on the second page of it, under -- at the top of the page, under item F, where it says in the last -- that that item: "Team Knin report that continuing restriction of movement in trying to get to Benkovac and Obrovac. They were told by the policija on the check-points that they could only get to these places with the written permission from General Gotovina." Let me ask you: Do you remember being prevented from going to Obrovac and Benkovac on the 10th of August, the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were prevented from going there at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now move to P1288 which is in tab 16 of your binder. And right before -- in the paragraph item 2(b) right before the item 3, political situation. It says -- yeah, it's on the screen as well. It says: "As per order from the Croatian Ministry of Defence - and that report is from 12th of September from your team - only the Generals Gotovina Cermak can deal with the international organisation directly." Do you remember being told this?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Finally, in this sequence - just pausing the translation - and I will call up 65 ter 1045, which is at tab 51. And this is a daily report from Team Split on the 7th of August, and under item 2 it says: "We spoke about permission to go monitoring team N2 area, and he informed us that before clearance from Colonel General Gotovina we were not allowed to accomplish our tasks." Now, Mr. Hansen, based on your patrols in those times, what was your understanding of Mr. Gotovina's role and authority in the Krajina after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the General was -- was a -- a senior commanding officer, to which much was referred, and for us, basically it dealt with the restrictions of permissions to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr, Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 1045 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the assignment of exhibit numbers to documents that were tendered by the Prosecution motion of 25th of November 2008, the next exhibit number will be P2146, and that number will be assigned to this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, in your statement you also refer to times where you were stopped at a check-point and you called General Cermak from the check-point, and upon calling him, restrictions of movement were lifted. Now let me show you one of those examples, and that is P1294 marked for identification, and that is at tab 23 of your binder. It's a 15 September report from your team. And at the top, section B under FOM, freedom of movement, it says on our way to Donji Lapac, restriction of movement in Otric lifted only after phone call to General Cermak." Mr. Hansen, can you tell the Court approximately how many times you were stopped at the check-point and able to get through after calling General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult for me to remember the exact numbers. But in the very beginning we were restricted from moving around. Then upon arrival of General Cermak, I think it was in the middle of -- of August, we agreed that -- or we talked about the restrictions of moving around, and he agreed that we -- if we were faced with problems we could call him directly and he would be of assistance, and so we did, and I would assume that we did this maybe three, five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could have P1294 admitted into evidence. That was one of the attachments to the witness statement where there were objections for late disclosure, but that that document was, in fact, disclosed in March 2007. So if we could have that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will retain exhibit number P1294 but will now become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hansen, on those occasions where you were stopped at check-points, did you see military vehicles going through the check-points with what appeared to be looted goods without being stopped?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And was this a regular occurrence or an exceptional occurrence when you observed this?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a regular occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can now go to P895 which is in tab 18. Mr. Hansen, you meant General Gotovina on one occasion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we have the report from that date that will come up from your team, dated 20 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I may have called up the wrong number. P895.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just wait for the document to come on the screen so that everyone can follow. I'd like to thank Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now you talk about this meeting in item 2. And just to confirm, you were team leader K1, TL K1, that refers to yourself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says that you and the head of the RC and the deputy head of the CC met General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph : "Asked about the ongoing looting, arson, and harassment. The General's opinion is that police has to control the situation and Croatia is still a nation with a constitution, law, and order. Any persons committing crimes will be charged. However, a war is always followed by disasters, and now things are under control. The General has no objection for Serbs to live in Croatia. But he regards it as a human feeling to hate an enemy, who has burned, looted, and expelled one's family. The war will not be stopped by nice words of international organisations [sic]." Now, Mr. Hansen, what did you make of that statement from Mr. Gotovina that he regards it as "a human feeling to hate an enemy who has burned, looted, and expelled one's family"?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ARSK was a Serb occupied territory of Croatia, and at the time of the occupation in 1991, the majority of the Croat population were expelled from that area and facing kind of harassment and burning and looting, just like it happened in 1995. Sorry, in -- yeah, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hansen, do you have an independent recollection of this meeting with Mr. Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, today I'm not having any additional recollection apart from this report, and I believe that at the time we wrote the report, it's accurately reflected the deliberations of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your impression, based on that meeting with General Gotovina, of his authority at the time in the region?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically that he would expect civilian authorities to hold responsibility and authority for the development following the military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In this meeting, did you discuss with General Gotovina whether Croatian soldiers had been involved in these crimes?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. We presented our -- our own observations, and that included uniformed and military personnel being part and parcel of the looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what was General Gotovina's response to that?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I can refer to the text here, and he would excuse it with a human feeling of hate an enemy and, therefore, some level of revenge, probably, would be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you take the reference to "any persons committing crimes will be charged," did you understand that to cover both civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now change topics and move to -- let's keep this document. You remember visiting the Plavno valley, Mr. Hansen?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to item 4(a) at the bottom of this report on the same page. It says: "Today we visit Plavno valley. Situation is going worse." And there's a team comment: "Many cars patrolling today with a lot of stolen goods inside." End comment. And then it says: "In each hamlet we heard a lot of complaints due to looting, shooting, killing cattle, and no police protection up to now. Desperate people ... want to move to Serbia?" And let me show you another report, which is 65 ter 6994, that is at tab 46. And it's another report for Team K1, and under 2 it says: "Today we visited Plavno valley. Most of the people we met are getting more and more desperate due to the ongoing looting and harassment. They want to leave immediately to Serbia." Mr. Hansen, do you remember people in Plavno wanting to leave because of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have 65 ter 6994 tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P2147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I could now have please 65 ter 7025, which is tab 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hansen -- I'll just wait for the document to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Go to the third page of this document. Under item 3(e), it mentions that the chief of police in Knin told team K1 that the main police task is to protect people and their property and to perform traffic control and that in his opinion, the state of manpower is adequate and sufficient to fulfill the task by manning check-points and doing mobile patrols in remote areas. Then the very next paragraph under 4(a), it says that team K1 heard that three houses had been set on fire, and there was -- there were looting activities as well done by both HV and civilians, and there are some car plates listed. Before I ask you my question about Plavno and the check-points, let me go to 65 ter 7027, which is tab 44. And under 2, political situation, you write on 23 September, your team writes: "Today we saw a lot of traffic in Plavno, and for the first time we noticed military police team, three people with a car plate. The man that was in charge was captain of the 72nd brigade and that that MP team was patrolling. And in Basinac which is in Plavno valley, the K1 that is you and the military police team, both were witnesses of looting our professional soldiers." Let me just ask you first, what did you mean by professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that they were uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then you talk to these MPs and you say: "We spoke with the military police, and they told us that the check-point is inform about the above mentioned." Now to your knowledge, Mr. Hansen, was anything done to these soldiers that were looting in Plavno?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, nothing was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I could have 65 ter 7025 and 7027 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 7025 will become Exhibit P2148; and 65 ter 7027 will become Exhibit P2149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And both are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, the last major topic I want to explore with you -- there will be a very short one at the end. But the last major one is the destruction, the burning that you observed and reported after Operation Storm. In your statement and reports, you mention a number of times observing the burning of Serb homes in Sector South. We will now go through all of these incidents with you, just talk about some specifics, and then I want to focus on more general aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could first have 65 ter 7009 which is at tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is 9 August daily report. And on the third page of that report, you state: "ECMM in Knin reports that the very same acts committed in Autumn 1991 are now being repeated. Looting and burning of the surrounding villages continue in the plain view of UN and international organisations." Then there is a comment. Says: "The burning of the Krajina Serb farming resources effectively prevents them to return in larger numbers. Individual small farming constitutes the basic livelihood of Krajina Serbs." Mr. Hansen, did you draft this comment?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure, but I could certainly have done it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you agree with what is said in the comment?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I totally agree with the content of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have 65 ter 7009 evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2150 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now go to P935 which is at tab 8. This is a weekly report from the 13th of August. If we could go to the bottom of the second page. It says all teams in the former Serb-held territory have been continuously reporting that apart from the Croat minority village of Podlapac and the old Croat town of Drnis, almost all towns throughout the area have suffered much burning of houses. And some of the smaller villages and towns of Donji Lapac and Kistanje have had every single building burnt out." Mr. Hansen, during your time in Sector South, did you visit any Croat villages?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could the Court if you remember the name of the village and where it was in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- at a few occasions I visited a small hamlet, Siveric I think the name was, about 30, 25, 30 kilometres from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you visit this village after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was that village destroyed?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We'll come back to Kistanje in a few seconds. But if we move two pages further in this document, on the last page. The last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly the name of the small hamlet was what, Mr. Hansen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it as Siveric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Than would be spelled as far as you recollect how.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: S-i-v-e-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: On the last page of this document, it states: "Rural areas and villages have been systematically burnt and looted. Only the odd hamlet and previously Croat village remaining untouched. Knin town and immediate surroundings have suffered only superficial damage and are therefore the only area where displaced persons can be expected to re-establish themselves." Mr. Hansen, can you tell the Court what you observed during your patrols in terms of destruction, when comparing the rural areas to the larger towns such as Knin, Obrovac, and Benkovac? What was the difference, if any?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a consistent pattern developed which saw urban centres left without any structural damage, very much in -- in contrast to the rural areas which were all burned and destroyed. So you had really a remarkable difference between destruction and preservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And at that time, based on your observations, what did you conclude about this difference?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it appeared as it was an outstanding difference, it appeared to be a part of a wider plan, although I have never seen a plan or been informed about a plan. But it certainly turned -- in our evaluation, it turned out to be a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's go back to P830 which was at tab 6 of your binder. That was a 10th August daily report where there was a mention of General Gotovina at a check-point. And I said we're going to come gook it, so let's go to the second page. In item 4(d) there are two incidents that you report. In Kistanje you report the burning by a soldier there uniform. And also in Kosovo you report six uniformed soldiers that were seen going house to house setting fires. Mr. Hansen, were you present in both of those locations to witness these burnings?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Court what you saw, taking them one at a time. Let's start with Kistanje, and then we'll talk about what you saw in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, upon entering Kistanje we saw a military lorry parked in front of a grocery store. And inside the store a uniformed person was carrying a jerry-can, and while we continued our journey, we returned some 15 minutes later, and the grocery store was -- was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what you saw in Kosovo with the six uniformed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Upon return to -- to Knin, we saw just south of the town quite a development of smoke, and we decided to go there and see what was happening. And a few kilometres south of -- of Knin, we saw quite a number of farm houses being set ablaze by this group of people, which is referred to in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how -- how was these group of farm houses being set ablaze? How did you see the group of uniformed soldiers doing this?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were -- they were moving around in -- in a jeep and -- well, moving from house to house and setting it ablaze. We could see that from a distance, and we even photographed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to 65 ter 7015 which is at tab 32 of your binder. This is a special report of destruction in the former RSK. Under item 2, tactics, it says: "The main technique was performed first by HV soldiers followed by returning displaced persons and refugees was looting and then burning the houses. Different measures were seen from simple burning with wood and paper to large organised actions, done by regular, commanded HV units with jerrycans and petrol. The driving force behind this systematic devastating is assessed to be government and military orders. 70 to 80 per cent of the houses are only consisting of walls and holes. So to live in this house is only possible only after complete restoration and re-building. The only villages, towns which were not heavily damaged were the chosen new accomodation for the Croatian displaced persons. These are Knin," as a showcase; there's a description of Vrlika, Drnis, Benkovac, Obrovac," and so on. And, Mr. Hansen, is this general description of the burning in Sector South consistent with what you observed in the course of all your patrols?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the urban/rural disparity, it certainly is a scenario I can confirm, and with urban centres being saved and the rural areas being torched. I'm not so sure about the 70, 80 per cent of houses consistently being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What about the manner in which the burning was performed ranging from simple burning with wood and paper to large organised actions done by regular commanded HV units with jerrycans and petrol?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, referring to my last statement, I can confirm that torching was also conducted by uniformed personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: MR. President, can I have 65 ter 7015 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear no objections expressed. Therefore, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2151 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me move to a slightly different topic, staying within destruction. Let me show -- that's about the status of churches in Sector South. Let me show you a few documents quickly, and then I will ask you a few questions on that series. Let's start with P806 which is tab 4. That's an 8 August daily report. On the last page of this report at item B it says: "Team Knin report that, although there are many chapels destroyed, the Orthodox church seems to be untouched and has a military policija guard outside." Then I want to go to the next tab, tab 5 which is P933. That is the report for the next day. And on the second page you can see an a few churches being mentioned, the one in Kosovo it says -- there was a sign on the door saying, Do not touch, HV. Then two days later, P934, now we're at tab 7. Page 3 again, under item B at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we go to the third page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At B, it says that a policija guard was guarding the Orthodox church next to the graveyard. Then I want to show you P951, which is not in your binder, which is a list of churches prepared by ECMM and their status. Team K1 in Knin, and it lists a number of churches and their status. Then finally the last document before I ask you my question, is 65 ter 7024, which is at tab 41 which is a supplement to the 9th, to the report we just saw. And it lists a number of churches and Orthodox churches, particularly that were not damaged in these towns. Now, Mr. Hansen, what was the general situation of Orthodox churches in the villages that you visited after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were intact and -- and as it is mentioned in some of the reports that they were even sign-posted by the HV and with the information to leave them intact and not target them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have 65 ter 7024 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2152 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can now go to your diary, which is P1292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that this would be the right moment to return the diary, the original, to Mr. Hansen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I thought that was going to be done yesterday. But, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw it is still here so ... Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Feel free to refer to the original or to the English portions, whichever is more convenient for my question. On page 8 of the English, the entry for the 9th of August, that is the day where we just saw the report where we noted the sign, Do not touch, on the door of the Kosovo church. In the second full paragraph you write: "The Croats have been sensible enough not to touch the churches in the villages. In some cases mine warning signs have been put up, in other places signs saying, Do not touch, Croatian army. Clearly the units have been told to keep their hands off religious buildings, and they have followed the order. They know that destroying churches would resinate all over the world. Yet the churches are the only thing they have actually kept their hand off." Mr. Hansen, do you still agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Next page of your diary, the entry of the 10th of August, towards the bottom you say: "All the churches we came across were intact, and it appears that General Gotovina has issued orders to troops to keep their hands off." And in your third statement at paragraph 22, you refer to this specific entry in your diary, and you stated: "Since all other structures were burning and it was no secret that General Gotovina was the person responsible for the military operations, we just assumed that it was not a coincidence that the churches were left standing and that he must have specifically instructed troops not to destroy or damage them." Mr. Hansen, is that still your assessment today?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my assessment today also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to 65 ter 7012, which is at tab 29 of your collection. At the bottom of the first page -- the top of the second page, under political situation, it says: "President Tudjman spokeswoman said that uncontrollable troops and civilians were responsible for these actions, and that's the methodical destruction of Krajina Serb homes. But that the UN has called into question the sincerity of the Croatian governments appeal to civilian Serbs to stay." Mr. Hansen, at the time did ECMM share the same view as the UN on this issue?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 7012 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have P1287 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is at tab 14. This is a weekly assessment. If we can go to the third page of that weekly assessment under humanitarian situation. And it says: "The burning of Serb properties and the looting is still ongoing in the former sectors north and south. Soldiers and civilians have been seen laden with booty. ECMM has logged and recorded all witnessed incidents, as have a number of other international organisations. These activities have been reported to the Croatian authorities who have attributed them to unruly elements, and in one case a senior HV officer was heard to reply when asked why was a professional army doing this, Why do people drink and drive? Then it states the inference from the lack of control over these elements is that the HV is largely uncontrollable, or that by their inaction the highest ranking HV officers and Croatian government officials are, in fact, condoning the activities of their soldiers and civilians. The implications of these events are that they send a clear message that Serbs are not welcome in Croatia, even if they are accepted by the government. The Croatian people will not tolerate any further co-existence with a Serb minority." And you touch on that briefly in your statement at paragraph 16, where you -- you say that you assume that the destruction was all part of a higher plan, or it is an implicit acceptance of it. Before asking my question, I also want to focus on your diary on this same issue which is on page 11, the entry for the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that is P1292. Actually, it's the entry for the 12th of August, right above the entry for the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It says: "We saw yet more houses being set alight. There is no longer any doubt that this is an official policy to prevent the Serbs from moving back in. The only tragedy is that the western press doesn't have a clue this is going on." Now, Mr. Hansen, we have seen a few conclusions in the weekly assessment and in this diary. Can you tell the Chamber what were the facts an observations that you made that brought you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, a systematic pattern of -- of looting of all property, the destruction of rural property, and preservation of urban appropriate, and the fact that the Serb population at this point simply were not there anymore. And led us to the conclusion that there may have been a wider plan that supported this scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hansen. The last very short topic I want to address with you is the -- the return of Serbs or, rather, the problems they faced in returning. The first document I want to show you is 65 ter 7021, which is at tab 38 of your binder. And it says under political situation, item 2: "About two persons, a Serb man and Croat wife coming from Zagreb, and they told ECMM that they recently went to Belgrade in order to bring back their parents who is fled Serbia, but they couldn't. The problem is that the parents need papers to enter Croatia which can only be delivered in Croatia themselves and nobody else, and according to them Croatian authorities are doing this on purpose in order to prevent Serbs from coming back to their houses." At that time, Mr. Hansen, when you were in Sector South is that something that you knew about that other Serbs told you about, the problem they had in crossing the border?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time it was a problem very much in the earlier stages, but later on it developed to a major issue. And the core of the issue is that -- that the Serb population were asked to apply for citizenship to return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were they allowed to apply for citizenship before coming first back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, before returning to Croatia they were supposed to apply for citizenship. But this -- this administration was not supported by the setting up of facilities that could support the applications at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, and just for the record, Mr. President, what we see in item 3(c), the two persons being killed in Palanka, Kuzman Pijac and Dusan Savic are part of the Prosecution's clarification killings, and those are victim numbers 253 and 254. And if I can have 65 ter 7021 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections by any of the Defence teams. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2154 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can now go to 65 ter 7023 which is at tab 40. On the second page of this document under item 3, humanitarian situation, there is some destruction mentioned, but there's also that third paragraph that I want to focus on, where it says that: "The Croatian government is preparing a law which allows displaced persons to be accommodated in abandoned houses if the owner does claim his property within 30 days. This law may open ways to illegally expropriate Serbs who fled the area." Now, Mr. Hansen, were you aware at the time that such a law was about to be passed or that was being passed?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not personally aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At the time did you hear about such a law that was going to be -- or that it was in the making?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we heard rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the witness said he didn't know anything about it, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he said he was not personally aware of it, and I think that Mr. Hedaraly is seeking clarification what that exactly means under those circumstances. Did you hear about it at the time, or did you see any documents? Could you explain what you meant by that you were not personally aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By mentioning that I was not personally aware is a phrase that I use because I did not see any documentation, I did not see any public information about it, but we heard rumours at the time that this was a law in the making, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rumours coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in -- there was a lot of rumours going on everywhere at this time so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're not able to identify who exactly spoke about it under what circumstances and with what authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when it says that the law allows displaced persons to be accommodated, what you heard about that, that would be Croat displaced persons from 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have 65 ter 7023 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 7023 has been admitted, I believe, as 2152, if I'm not mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, 2154 was 7024 on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that there are no objections, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 7023.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will become Exhibit P2155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the last document I want to show you, Mr. Hansen, is 65 ter 7011, which is at tab 28 of your binder. This is a 14 August report. I want to go -- actually, on the second page we can see under former Sector North and Sector South it says: "In former sectors north and south, the Croatian civilian police appears to be replacing regular HV units which are retained from the barracks." But that's not the question I want to ask you about. It is it on the third page, the next page, the middle, it has an announcement from the head of the Croatian government committee for the return of displaced persons, Minister Radic. And under item B it says: "Displaced persons can also return to free houses and flats." And then there's a comment saying: "Free houses and flats can be interpreted as the homes of thousands of Serbs who fled Croatia following Operation Storm." And then two paragraphs later: "The systematic destruction and burning of large areas in the southern part of former Sector South is also continuing. Houses have been burnt in practically every town of former Sector South (except certain villages with a Croatian minority). In some smaller villages and towns, every single building has been destroyed." Now my question for you refers to the earlier portion about the free houses and flats. At the time when you were in Sector South, did you observe Croatian -- Croat displaced persons from 1991 moving into Serb abandoned houses after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any -- any settlement or return of Croats to settle in abandoned Serb property. We saw a lot of what I would call tourism where people came to see the area -- where Croats came to see the place, but they did not stay and returned to from wherever they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 7011 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, Madam Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2156 is admitted into evidence. Whenever it appears on the transcript that I say no objections, that is not because I decided that there are no objections, but it reflects what happens in the courtroom. That is, when looking at Defence teams from their body language, I deduce there are no objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one quick housekeeping matter regarding exhibits. If we can have P1293 vacated. That was the aerial photo marked by the witness. In court he added a marking and that has become P1299, I believe. So there is no more need for P1293. We can just keep the photograph with the additional marking, as opposed to keeping both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the original marking can be clearly distinguished from the later marking which was very limited and was just about a house, I think, in addition to already numbered markings which were assigned Roman numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked photograph is P1298.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will check that. Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic, for this correction. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this time I would like the diary, P1292 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you had an opportunity to look at the original. Apart from this aspect, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing further than have been presented previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the Chamber will further consider the objections already presented by the Defence, and I think, as I said before, at the end of the -- at the conclusion of the testimony of this witness, the Chamber will decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The only remaining item is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing is now that it then -- it is uploaded because it has not yet received a number when I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It received a MFI number because I was going to refer to it, and that was P1292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I must have missed that. So it keeps the status of marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. The last item, Your Honour, is a few bar table documents. I sent them yesterday to counsel. There were the three from yesterday, P1295, up to and including 1297. And there were additional ones, 65 ter 7022 which relates to killing number 156, and 65 ter 3532 which relates to the events in Grubori, scheduled killing number 4. The portions have been provided in the spreadsheet that was sent yesterday. I would move for all five of these to be admitted as well as the newspaper article, but I understand those are all bar table submissions, so it's whenever it's convenient for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The five documents just referred to by Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have not had a chance to look at those, and certainly not in the context presented here. I will take a look at those as quickly as possible given the fact that they are coming across as a bar table submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then numbers will be assigned to them and they will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the first series of three, 1295, 1296, 1297, those being 65 ter numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Those are P numbers marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are P numbers. They are already --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The last two ones are the ones that need P numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 7022. Yes, you're right. Madam Registrar, 65 ter 7022 will be marked for identification as ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2157, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And 65 ter 3552.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2158, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Kehoe, when could we hear from you and from other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the beginning of the week, Your Honour, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the beginning of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a small error. I think you stated 3552, and I think it's 3532, just so that we don't get confused, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not a doctor, but my handwriting is just as bad as that from doctors. Thank you, Mr. Cayley. So it is 65 ter 3532 that has now been assigned P number 2158. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This concludes the Prosecution's examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I think it would be practical to have the break now because otherwise we would have to stop after five minutes. Are the Defence teams confident that the invitation to conclude the testimony of this witness today is achievable?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will go first. Your invitation is very welcomed, and I will in fact be considerably less than three hours, so I think we will be able to hold Mr. Kehoe responsible for the fact that we end up with time running out at the end, but certainly I think all three counsel will be finished. I will be a matter of an hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I estimate that I will be one session at the most which is about an hour and a half, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber felt more or less compelled yesterday to instruct for a very short lunch break. Now, there are two options: Either we say we will easily deal with the matter, let's take more time for lunch. We also could prefer to have not too late a finish today. Could I hear who are the lunch freaks and who are the earlier weekend freaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm an early weekend freak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm a lunch freak, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm just a freak, Your Honour. For me, I'm not worried, Your Honours. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, do you have any preference. I don't know whether you have any travel arrangements which would make it more attractive for you to leave early.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My key concern would be our ability to complete my presence here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no -- there is not pressing need to rush to airports or trains or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no preference as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will finally decide this very important matter, but not until after Mr. Hedaraly, the Prosecution has had an opportunity to express itself on the matter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The Prosecution will leave it up to the Chamber, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to take you back very briefly to a response that you gave to my learned friend Mr. Hedaraly. When he asked you about the period between 1991 and 1995, when the Krajina was in fact an occupied part of Croatia, occupied by the Serbs, do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying that after 1991 the Croatian population was attacked, their property was burned and looted, and they were expelled from this area of Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not there at the time, but you are right, in the sense that the majority Croat population were expelled from the RSK occupied areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in August of 1995, after Knin was retaken, many of these people who been expelled returned to the Krajina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right in the sense that during my time in the aftermath of the operation, I saw many civilians returning to the area not to settle at this point, but I think I called it tourism before. So they were there to somehow, I would assume, check property to see what it was like after some years of absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Knin fell much more quickly than the Croatians expected it to. It fell, to them, in a much quicker fashion than they had expected, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But certainly the -- we had the impression that -- that the military operation succeeded in a much faster pace than originally anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the aftermath of the military operation to retake Knin was a fairly disorganised situation. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these Croatian civilians who were returning, these tourists as you call them, were returning into this disorganisation; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these individuals -- did you speak to any of these people, the returning Croatian civilians?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did any of your colleagues speak to these people?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you describe them, at least the people you saw even if you didn't speak to them, that they were angry after having been absent from the region for several years?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in one instance, I recall a person being angry because I met that person. But apart from this, I would assume that people were simply interested in -- in having a look into an area they lived in before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these civilians that you saw returning, do you know whether any of these individuals were the individuals that were, later on in the month of August, involved in looting property in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can now talk a little bit about Mr. Cermak. Would I be right in saying that it was your impression that Mr. Cermak attached importance to a good relationship with the European Community monitoring mission? And I have an exhibit that I can show to you if you want to refresh your memory from the time.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think this is an accurate description of the invitation to a cooperation, and I remember an invitation that -- from General Cermak that somehow invited for a level of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you regarded him as the point of contact for ECMM within Knin.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, for civilian affairs, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that his door was always open as far as can you remember to the ECMM. If you wanted to see him, you could?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm right in saying also that at some stage he tried to find you accommodation in Knin, didn't he? I don't think he was successful, but I think he made an offer of trying to find you accommodation.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true in the sense that we -- we informed General Cermak about our difficulties in identifying a suitable place for our office, and upon this information he offered his assistance in identifying a suitable place, and so following this he assigned two liaison officers to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And did you eventually find accommodate addition or not?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where eventually did you base your headquarters in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually we agreed with a -- with a landlord of one of the monitors to turn his accommodation into an office base.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to turn to another subject matter with you, and that is the title and function of General Cermak. Now, in your first two statements, you refer to Mr. Cermak as the military governor. I won't show those to you; I don't think there is any dispute about that with the Prosecution. But I would like you to look at your statement of April of 2008, and that's P1285.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we can have page 4 of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That would be tab 3 in the -- if I don't mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, no, please. Thank you, that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 you'll see the second sentence reads: "The first meeting occurred upon his invitation sometime in the middle of August, although I cannot be sure of the exact date. We understood from that meeting that he was acting as the civilian governor." So in this statement you state that he is the civilian governor. Now, before I ask you any questions, I want to show you a number of other ECMM documents that you've admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we can please have P2153.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't know what the tab is, Mr. Hansen, but certainly will you see it on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if, please, we could go to the -- the first page at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you'll see there that it states that: "The restriction of movement which was reported on 16 August came to an end following a meeting with the commander of the operation zone, General Cermak." So there we see ECMM describing Mr. Cermak by another kind of title.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to P815. And if we could go, please, to the second page of that document, I'm sorry, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is, in fact, Mr. Hansen, a report by one of your colleagues from Denmark, Mr. Soren Liborius. And you will see in paragraph 3 that Mr. Cermak there is described as the commander of the Knin Military District. Do you see that? It's paragraph 3 at the bottom, Living conditions in the former Krajina.

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now please go to P1286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, what we saw on our screen, the three pages, says what the military commander did. But it does not identify Mr. Cermak as such. So with full respect for the answer of the witness, what you suggest it's described there, I do not find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour, by I think Mr. Liborius actually referred to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But not in this portion, the name of Mr. Cermak does not appear in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can he go to P12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's just you asked the witness whether that is what is described there, isn't it? Whether Mr. Liborius describes this, and I have some difficulties in understanding how the witness could find that there without any further reference to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will move to another exhibit which is clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: P1286. And can we go to the second page. Can we move to the bottom of that page. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And there you can see if you look at the last but one paragraph, it says comment: "The military commander and administrator of Knin, General Cermak, stated earlier that these soldiers are under his personal protection." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, it's only the title that I'm interested in. And let's not include because of the comments of the Presiding Judge, commander, Knin Military District. But it appears, doesn't it, from these documents that there was a certain degree of either disagreement or confusion in ECMM about the official title of Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what you have presented there, it stands out that there is a different -- a difference in understanding of his responsibility, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was amongst your colleagues. There was a problem in the perception of what his actual function was. You had differing views amongst ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I would think it's fair that from my dealings with General Cermak we were having -- what we were talking to him about was in all instances about civilian affairs, restrictions of movement, the operation of the check-points, and, as such, well, he was in uniform and was introduced as General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that he was in a uniform. Did he strike you as a military kind of man or not?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. Not really. A very different character than I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to describe him as a civilian in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, did you know that the position of military governor did not in fact exist within the Croatian governmental scheme either in the military or the police or in the government generally? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you ever made aware of the fact that in fact General Cermak was appointed as the commander of Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now talk a little bit about the resources that General Cermak had at his disposal. Were you aware that in August there were only ten individuals working in his headquarters in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about the organisation of his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that for the functions for the civilian affairs that you were referring to that he had very limited resources at his disposal from what you could see as a military man?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our impressions were very much so that he had extremely few resources at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And by that we're now talking about personnel or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And from your observations of him functioning in Knin, would it also be fair to say that he was simply overwhelmed with claims for his time and his resources?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit now about what you could observe General Cermak doing, so what functions, what kinds of activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could please show you D299.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now there are many of these documents, Mr. Hansen, but I'm only going to show you a couple from the time-period when you were present in Knin. And here can you see that this is a request to General Forand to basically recover damaged or abandoned vehicles in Knin. Do you remember who General Forand was?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you remember him as the UNCRO south military commander?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing many abandoned and damaged vehicles in the streets in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now please move to D298.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is another request of the 8th of August to General Forand from Colonel General Cermak to help restore the water works in Knin? Do you remember at the time that there was a problem with the supply of water after Knin was retaken?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there was a problem with all public utilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please move to the next document, which is 2D03-004 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see that this is a request from Mr. Cermak to have the assistance of UNCRO repairing the electricity power grid?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall at the time that there were problems with electricity supply after the fall of Knin?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this could be an exhibit number. I don't think there should be any objections from the Prosecution. It's one of their documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D1270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1270 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could please have 2D03-0007.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you'll see that this is a request from Mr. Cermak of the 9th of August, requesting that the area around the Knin hospital be cleared and asking for the provision of an excavator in order to allow the hospital to resume its work. Do you recall at the time that there was debris around the hospital that needed clearing or not?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that the general area around the hospital was impacted during the early days of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If there's no objections from the Prosecution, Your Honour, I'd ask for that document to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly nods that there are no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And finally on this, if we could please have document 65 ter 851.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And here you see a decision by Mr. Cermak to charge the commander of the HV materiel supplies with opening grocery stores, cafes, and cake shops in Knin on the 10th of August. Do you recall shops and businesses reopening, even in a limited fashion at that time, Mr. Hansen?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to show you any other documents, but we've seen from these documents the kind of work that Mr. Cermak was involved in, water, electricity, re-opening shops, cleaning debris. Was that the impression that you were left with? Was that what you saw his function was in Knin?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that we were -- that this was our impression then, in addition to our difficulties with moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And we'll come to that in a moment. But in essence he was the man responsible for essentially rebuilding its early stages, the civilian infrastructure in and around Knin so that society could get working again?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if I could please show you P1288 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I have just been reminded that that document needs an exhibit number. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1272 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If, please, Madam Registrar, we could have P1288. And if we could please go to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hansen, if you can see that document clearly on the screen, and you go about a third of the way down that paragraph, you will see it begins: "Now five weeks." Do you see that? Sorry, I know it's not very clear. It's ...

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can just read that. "Now five weeks after the operation, we still see houses set on fire and extensive looting is ongoing. Also that individuals seem [sic] to select houses and simply move in. According to our opinion, there is an police task here, and too little has been done to prevent torching, looting, and individual settlement." Now, the question I have for you is this: At this time it was the ECMM view that the civilian police were responsible for stopping the burning and the looting that was taking place. Yes?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware at this time of the structure of the civilian police, the hierarchy, who was in charge, who the subordinates were, within the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could look, please, at P962. Now this is the structure --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could just go up a little bit please to show the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is the Ministry of the Interior organisation for the Knin region. You see at the top the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak. Now, you can take it from me that Mr. Cermak does not appear in that hierarchical structure at all. I don't think there is any dispute from the Prosecution on that issue. We don't need to go through all of it, although I would just ask to you look at the box at the top which has the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak in it because I have a few questions related to an incident that you referred to in your statement. Now, if you can please go to P1285 which is your statement. I think that maybe is tab 3 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, is it tab 3? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it's tab 3 in your binder. And if you could go to paragraph 17. Now, you'll see in the first sentence there, you say: "I don't know whether Cermak really had the power to stop [sic] looting and burning, if he was sincere when he was stating that he would try to control it." Is it fair to say that you formed the view at the time in the Knin area that Mr. Cermak was not a major influential figure, that he was a minor player. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, in terms of guaranteeing law and order in this chaotic time, it would be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you didn't believe, did you, at this time, that he had the authority to stop looting in the region, did you?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not, and certainly his actions did not control it, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let me just show you one exhibit which is D59. And this you can see is a newspaper article, and I'll just let you -- can you read that all right, Mr. Hansen?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know this is an article that was actually produced while you were on probably well-earned leave back home in Denmark. But were you aware that Mr. Cermak had actually publicly condemned the looting and the burning that was taking place in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not seen this article before, but certainly in our conversations he expressed views of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when he spoke to you he basically condemned the looting and burning that was taking place in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, did he.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just very briefly talk about freedom of movement. And if I can take you to Exhibit 1284. And this, I believe, is tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it's really so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go, please, I'm sorry, Madam Registrar, to the second page of that document. Sorry, Madam Registrar, if we could go to the next page. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, and just so we're clear immediately where we're going, Mr. Hansen, this is in fact a correction that I'd like you to make to your own statement. And you will see immediately what I mean when I show you the report. Now, you state in the second paragraph that you have been shown a sitrep of the 17th of August. And you say that you are the co-author of that report. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIG MARKER HANSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph: "The experiences that we the previous day were restricted from moving through the town of Vrlika in the south. Immediately we visited the governor, Ivan Cermak and complained about restriction of movement. During our stay in his office, he did what was obviously in his power by phoning directly to the police station concerned and asked them to guarantee the ECMM and international organisations freedom of movement in that specific area?" I want you to directed your mind to the part of the sentence that says "by phoning directly to the police station," if you can remember that.
